title: Chemicals in Chlorinated Drinking Water Linked to Increased Risk of Uterine Cancer, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A 25-year study tracking more than 53,000 California women found that common disinfection byproducts in tap water, including trihalomethanes and haloacetic acids, are associated with significantly elevated uterine cancer risk.
body:
• A National Cancer Institute study published in JAMA Network Open found that disinfection byproducts in chlorinated tap water are linked to higher uterine cancer risk.
  • Women with the highest exposure to trihalomethanes showed an 18% increased risk of uterine cancer and a 23% higher risk of endometrioid tumors.
  • Haloacetic acids were associated with an 86% higher risk of nonendometrioid tumors, a more aggressive form of the disease.
  • The chemicals act as endocrine disruptors that bind to estrogen receptors, a known pathway for uterine cancer development.

A landmark study led by the National Cancer Institute has established a direct link between long-term exposure to chemicals in chlorinated drinking water and a significantly higher risk of uterine cancer in women, adding uterine cancer to a growing list of health concerns tied to common water treatment byproducts.

The research, published July 22 in JAMA Network Open, tracked 53,100 California educators over 25 years as part of the California Teachers Study cohort. The study identified disinfection byproducts — specifically trihalomethanes (THMs) and haloacetic acids (HAAs) — as the primary culprits. These chemicals form when chlorine, the most widely used water disinfectant, reacts with organic matter in water.

THMs and Chloroform: The Sharpest Risks

The findings, led by Dr. Rena R. Jones of the NCI, reveal a dose-dependent relationship between DBP exposure and uterine cancer. Women with the highest long-term exposure to total THMs showed an 18% increased risk of developing uterine cancer overall and a 23% higher risk of developing endometrioid tumors, the most common form of uterine cancer.

Chloroform, the most abundant individual THM in chlorinated water, showed the strongest single-chemical association, with a 27% higher risk for endometrioid tumors. The five most common HAAs were linked to an alarming 86% higher risk of developing nonendometrioid tumors, a more aggressive and harder-to-treat subtype.

"We report novel associations between the highest DBP levels and endometrial cancer that warrant future evaluation."

— Dr. Rena R. Jones, National Cancer Institute

Building on Earlier Evidence

The California findings align with an earlier study conducted by Jones and colleagues using data from the Iowa Women's Health Study, which followed more than 10,500 postmenopausal women. That study found women with the highest average concentrations of THMs had a twofold increased risk of endometrial cancer, and those with elevated HAA5 levels faced an 84% higher risk.

The Iowa study also found that associations with THMs were stronger among women who had used hormone replacement therapy, suggesting a potential interaction between external hormonal factors and DBP exposure.

How the Chemicals May Cause Harm

Researchers noted that THMs and HAAs act as endocrine disruptors, binding to estrogen receptors and causing hormonal dysregulation — a well-established pathway for uterine cancer development. Animal studies have previously shown that ingestion of DBPs can lead to persistent elevated levels of serum estradiol and suppression of progesterone.

The threat extends beyond the kitchen tap. THMs are volatile and can be inhaled during hot showers or absorbed through skin contact during bathing or dishwashing, making cumulative exposure effectively constant for those on chlorinated water supplies.

What It Means for Millions of Women

Uterine cancer is the most common gynecological cancer in the United States, and incidence rates have been rising. While established risk factors include obesity and certain types of hormone replacement therapy, the role of environmental contaminants like DBPs has been understudied.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's maximum contaminant level for total THMs, set at 80 parts per billion, was established in the 1990s based primarily on evidence related to bladder cancer. These findings suggest the regulatory framework may need updating to account for newly identified cancer endpoints.

For the Indian diaspora, the study carries particular relevance. While municipal water treatment standards vary widely across India, chlorination remains the dominant disinfection method in most Indian cities, and DBP monitoring is far less rigorous than in the United States.

Looking Ahead

The researchers called for replication studies in other populations and further investigation into specific DBP compounds. Safer alternatives to chlorination, such as ultraviolet light and ozonation, exist but have not been widely adopted due to cost and infrastructure constraints. The new findings add urgency to that conversation.
